Press `S` for speaker notes, `O` for the slide overview, `?` for all shortcuts.

Feedback Delay Networks (FDNs) are the workhorse of efficient artificial
reverberation. This tutorial builds one from first principles, analyses what
makes it sound good or bad, and then optimises it with gradients — using
[**pyFDN**](https://artificial-audio.github.io/pyFDN/), an open-source Python
toolbox released at DAFx 2026.

**No prior experience with FDNs is required.** You should be comfortable with
Python and with basic DSP: filtering, convolution, and what a pole is.

## Before you arrive

Install the toolbox and the notebook extras:

```bash
# any environment manager works — uv shown here
uv venv --python 3.11
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install "pyfdn[examples]"
```

Then clone the repository for the notebooks and check the install:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/artificial-audio/pyFDN
cd pyFDN
python -c "import pyFDN; print(pyFDN.__version__)"
marimo edit examples/
```

`pyfdn[examples]` installs `marimo`, `matplotlib`, `plotly` and — via
[`flamo`](https://github.com/gdalsanto/flamo) — PyTorch. That last one is a
large download, so do it on hotel wifi rather than in the room.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**If the install does not work**, come anyway. Every notebook is
[rendered on the website](https://artificial-audio.github.io/pyFDN/examples_gallery.html)
with its plots and audio, and needs nothing but a browser.
:::

## What we will cover

| Time  | Duration | Segment | Content |
| ----- | -------- | ------- | ------- |
| 0:00  | 15 min   | **What is an FDN?** | Structure, transfer function, poles. The three knobs — delays, feedback matrix, absorption — and the three properties they control: density, mixing, decay. |
| 0:15  | 15 min   | **pyFDN, the tour** | Package layout, the `FDNBuild` data class, the representation translators, and a reverb in five lines of code. |
| 0:30  | 25 min   | **Hands-on 1 — build an FDN** | Choose delay lengths, swap feedback matrices, prescribe a frequency-dependent $T_{60}$ and measure whether you got it. Listen at every step. |
| 0:55  | 20 min   | **Hands-on 2 — optimise an FDN** | Differentiable FDNs with FLAMO: train a colorless reverberator, match a measured room, and see where optimisation fails. |
| 1:15  | 10 min   | **Beyond the vanilla FDN** | Allpass, paraunitary and scattering FDNs; coupled rooms and multi-slope decay. Then real time: compiling a pyFDN design to FAUST with [`adac`](https://github.com/cucuwritescode/adac), stability-certified, and running it in the browser. |
| 1:25  | 5 min    | **Q&A** | And how to contribute. |

All of these live in [`examples/`](https://github.com/artificial-audio/pyFDN/tree/main/examples)
and are rendered in the
[examples gallery](https://artificial-audio.github.io/pyFDN/examples_gallery.html).

| Segment | Notebook |
| --- | --- |
| Tour | `example_process_fdn`, `example_vanilla_FDN` |
| Hands-on 1 | `example_vanilla_FDN`, `example_absorption_geq`, `example_delay_matrix_density` |
| Hands-on 2 | `example_train_colorless_FDN`, `example_colorless_FDN`, `example_rir_to_fdn` |
| Beyond | `example_paraunitary_fdn`, `example_scattering_fdn`, `example_coupled_rooms`, `example_multislope_rir_to_fdn` |
| Real time | `example_fdn_to_faust` |

## Presenters

**Sebastian J. Schlecht** is Associate Professor of Signal Processing at
Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg. His research covers
artificial reverberation, differentiable audio processing and spatial audio, and
he is the lead developer of pyFDN.

**Facundo Franchino** is a graduate student at MIT. His BEng work at the
University of York proposed structured pruning for feedback delay networks; his
interests are FDNs, real-time audio and machine listening.

## Optional, for the real-time segment

The FAUST demo needs no toolchain — the notebook builds a link that compiles the
generated DSP in your browser. If you want to go further:

```bash
pip install dawdreamer        # render the compiled FAUST offline and compare
brew install faust            # or grame.fr/downloads — for faust2juce / C++ output
```

Both are optional and the notebook degrades gracefully without them.

## Room requirements

- Projector and screen
- Audio playback for listening examples
- Power for participant laptops, ideally
